## Approach

For this assignment, I selected the New York Times Most Popular API to explore which newspaper sections appear most frequently among the 20 most emailed articles over a 30-day period. I chose this API because I wanted to better understand what types of articles readers are interested in sharing. My plan is to use R to connect to the API, retrieve the article information, and convert the JSON response into a tidy data frame. I will focus on the article titles, sections, publication dates, and rankings. I also plan to group the articles by section and count how many articles appear in each category to identify which sections are most represented.

One challenge I anticipate is working with the JSON response because some information may be nested or contain missing values. I will use the `jsonlite` and `dplyr` packages to extract and organize the data. Another potential challenge is authenticating the API request, so I will store my API key in an environment variable rather than including it directly in my code.

Data source: New York Times Most Popular API

https://developer.nytimes.com/docs/most-popular-product/1/overview

API endpoint:

https://api.nytimes.com/svc/mostpopular/v2/emailed/30.json

## Research question

Which New York Times sections have the most articles among the 20 most emailed articles in the past 30 days?

## API and request

I selected the New York Times Most Popular API to examine which newspaper sections appear most frequently among the most frequently among the most emailed articles. I used the following endpoint: `https://api.nytimes.com/svc/mostpopular/v2/emailed/30.json`. This endpoint retrieves the 20 most emailed articles over a 30-day period. The 30 in the URL specifies the period in days, while the api-key query parameter authenticates the request. For security, I stored my API key in an environment variable rather than including it directly in my code. 

## Request and tidy data frame

```{r}
library(httr)
library(jsonlite)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(knitr)


api_key <- Sys.getenv("NYT_API_KEY")

if (api_key == "") {
  stop("API key not found. Check your .Renviron file.")
}

# NYT Most Popular API endpoint
endpoint <- "https://api.nytimes.com/svc/mostpopular/v2/emailed/30.json"


response <- GET(
  endpoint,
  query = list(`api-key` = api_key),
  timeout(30)
)


stop_for_status(response)


json_data <- fromJSON(
  content(response, as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8"),
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)


if (is.null(json_data$results)) {
  stop("No article results were returned.")
}
```

```{r}
# Extract article information into a tidy data frame
articles <- lapply(seq_along(json_data$results), function(i) {
  article <- json_data$results[[i]]

  tibble(
    rank = i,
    title = if (is.null(article$title)) NA_character_ else article$title,
    section = if (is.null(article$section)) NA_character_ else article$section,
    published_date = if (is.null(article$published_date)) NA_character_ else article$published_date
  )
}) %>%
  bind_rows()

kable(
  head(articles),
  caption = "First Six Most Emailed NYT Articles"
)
```


## Analysis

```{r}

section_counts <- articles %>%
  count(section, name = "article_count") %>%
  arrange(desc(article_count))


kable(
  section_counts,
  caption = "Number of Most Emailed NYT Articles by Section"
)
```


The results show that the Opinion section had the most articles among the 20 most emailed New York Times articles, with 6 articles. Magazine, Science, U.S., and Well each had 2 articles, while Books, Food, Style, The Upshot, Travel, and Your Money each had 1 article. These findings suggest that Opinion articles were particularly prominent among the most emailed articles during the selected 30-day period. However, the results are limited to the 20 most emailed articles returned by the API and do not necessarily represent the popularity of all New York Times articles.


## Data Cleaning Decisions

The API returned data in JSON format, which I converted into an R list using the jsonlite package. Since the JSON response contains nested information, I extracted only the fields needed for my analysis: article title, section, publication date, and ranking. I assigned NA to any missing values to keep the data frame consistent. Finally, I grouped the articles by section and counted the number of articles in each section to determine which sections appeared most frequently among the most emailed articles.
